fields.h1: Build Restaurant Automation for the Front and Back of House
fields.hero_description: Create restaurant automation that sends pickup orders to the kitchen and turns the closing count into tomorrow's order.
fields.features_heading: What Restaurant Automation Runs Each Service
fields.features_subheading: Automation in restaurants takes over the steps a manager repeats every night. Menu, pricing, and hospitality calls stay with your team.
fields.feature_1:
Starts on a ticket, a count, or a swap

Connects to Square through its Orders API. A new online order, a saved closing count, or a shift request starts each run, and each run is saved as a row your team can search.
fields.feature_2:
Kitchen rules in the words a chef uses

Describe a rule the way it is said on the line, such as 86 the short rib on the ordering page when fewer than 6 portions are left. Emergent writes the check, and a prompt changes it.
fields.feature_3:
Items, pars, and suppliers in your database

Keeps menu items, par levels, suppliers, and staff in a database you own. Every workflow reads the same tables, and a new supplier or dish is one new row, not a rebuilt workflow.
fields.feature_4:
Messages to the manager on shift

Sends a Slack message or an email to whoever owns the decision tonight. If nobody answers in 20 minutes, a reminder goes out, and the request moves to the next manager on the list.
fields.feature_5:
No task cap on a Friday rush

Runs every ticket and every count through the same steps on the busiest night of your year. When a holiday weekend triples takeout volume, no task cap stops the extra runs.
fields.feature_6:
The code is yours to keep

Exports the full codebase to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can read every rule, add a delivery partner, and host the app wherever your other systems run.

fields.usecase_heading: Workflows Behind a Busy Week of Service
fields.tab_content_1:
Each 15-minute pickup window closes at 12 orders

Hollis Street Kitchen, a neighborhood restaurant, runs its own automated ordering system for pickup. Every ticket goes to the kitchen screen with its pickup time and to Square. Once a window holds 12, it disappears, and guests choose a later time. Cooks see the next ticket due at the top of the screen.
fields.tab_content_2:
Tonight's walk-in count becomes tomorrow's produce order

At close, the line cook counts the walk-in on a phone, item by item. The app compares each count with its par level, the minimum stock the kitchen keeps on hand, and orders the difference. Chef Lucinda Haskett approves the draft for Harbor Produce in Slack, and the supplier gets it by email.
fields.tab_content_3:
Swaps that cross 40 hours wait for the GM

A server who wants Saturday off picks a coworker. The app adds those hours to the coworker's workweek, because federal overtime rules start at a workweek longer than 40 hours. A swap within the limit goes onto the schedule. One that crosses it waits for Odell Prather, the general manager, in a Slack direct message.
fields.tab_content_4:
When Tuesday books under 45 covers by 2:00 PM

Tuesday is the slow night. At 2:00 PM the app checks the reservation book, and if fewer than 45 covers are booked, it emails the $39 prix fixe to guests who opted in. Anyone emailed in the last 14 days is skipped. Unsubscribes come off the list before the next send, and each email is logged on the guest's record.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to start restaurant automation with one shift task, test it against last week, then add the next workflow.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick one trigger and one rule
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Put items and pars on one sheet
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the job a manager does every night: counting the walk-in, building the produce order, fixing the schedule after a swap, deciding whether tonight needs a push. Write down who does each one today and how long it takes.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Choose the job that costs the most time and name what starts it, such as a saved closing count. Then write its rule with real numbers: which supplier, which par, who approves, and what happens if nobody answers by 6:00 AM.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Put every item on one sheet with its unit, par level, supplier, and order cutoff. Staff go on a second sheet with their roles and contact details. Workflows read these tables, and an item without a supplier is flagged instead of guessed.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Tell Emergent what starts the workflow, what each run writes, and who decides when a rule is crossed. Emergent builds the workflow, the phone screens a shift uses, and the database behind them. Change any step by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Replay last Friday's tickets and last week's counts before the app touches a live service. Compare each result with what your team did by hand, order by order. A busy night shows whether pickup windows close where the kitchen expects.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Keep the clipboard and the group text for one week while the app logs what it would have done. Each mismatch becomes a change to a rule. Switch over when a full week matches, closing shifts included.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Build the second workflow on the tables the first one already fills. Guest records from the ordering page become the list a slow-night email reads, and restaurant marketing automation starts with consent stored on each guest's row.

og.headline: Build restaurant automation for every shift
og.alt: Build restaurant automation for the front and back of house, with Emergent

faq_plan.a: Restaurant automation is software that runs the repeated jobs around service on rules you set. An online order reaches the kitchen with its pickup time, a closing count becomes a supplier order, and a shift swap is checked against overtime. Automation in restaurants here means software for that work. Kitchen robots and kiosks are hardware and sit outside it.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up restaurant automation?
faq_plan.a: Pick one job that happens every shift and write its trigger and its rule with real numbers. Then describe it in plain English to Emergent's AI automation builder, which builds the workflow along with the screens and database it needs. A prompt changes any step later. Before it touches a live night, replay a past week through it and compare each result with what the team did by hand.

faq_plan.q: Which software systems does a restaurant run on?
faq_plan.ref: What software do most restaurants use?
faq_plan.a: Most restaurants run a set of systems, not one product. Chowbus's guide names point-of-sale systems for managing transactions and kitchen display systems that replace paper tickets. Its list also covers online ordering and inventory management, along with scheduling software and reservation management.

faq_plan.q: What should marketing automation for restaurants send first?
faq_plan.a: Start with a message tied to something the restaurant already knows, such as a light booking night or a guest's first pickup order. A thank-you note the morning after a first order needs nothing but the order record. Keep restaurant marketing automation to guests who opted in. The same trigger-and-list pattern carries over to property management automation.

faq_plan.q: What should an automated ordering system for restaurants send to the kitchen?
faq_plan.a: Each ticket should carry the items with their modifiers and allergy notes, plus the guest's name and promised pickup time. Give allergy notes their own field instead of the free-text comment, and have the kitchen screen show them in red. An automated restaurant ordering system should also message the guest when the cook marks the ticket ready.

faq_plan.q: Which restaurant tasks should I automate first?
faq_plan.a: Start with jobs that run every shift where guests never see the result, such as the closing count and the produce order built from it. A mistake there costs a phone call to the supplier, not a guest's dinner. Move to guest-facing work like pickup ordering once the inside workflows have run clean for a week or two.

faq_plan.q: Can one restaurant automation run several locations?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if every table carries a location column from the start. Each location keeps its own par levels and supplier list, and the owner sees every site on one screen. Emergent keeps the data for all of them in one database you own. Add the column before the second site opens, in restaurants and in education workflow automation alike.

faq_plan.q: How do I stop restaurant automation from overordering produce?
faq_plan.a: Give each item a maximum order quantity next to its par level, and have the app flag any line above it instead of sending it. Compare each draft with the last four weeks of use, and hold any order above a dollar amount you set until the chef approves it. Treat a count entered as zero with suspicion, since a skipped shelf reads the same as an empty one.

faq_plan.q: What happens if a restaurant workflow fails in the middle of service?
faq_plan.a: Have the app log every run and alert the manager on shift when one fails. That way the gap is caught that night, not at the next delivery. Keep a paper fallback for each workflow, such as a printed par sheet, where the closing crew can find it. Because each run is saved, the manager can see which counts were missed and run only those again.

faq_plan.q: Who should own a restaurant automation once it is live?
faq_plan.a: Give each workflow one owner on the management team, such as the kitchen manager for supplier orders and the GM for scheduling. That person changes rules by prompting Emergent, and a new supplier cutoff never waits on a developer. On paid plans, the full code can be exported to your GitHub repository. Apply the same one-owner rule to agency workflow automation.
